I.     RECOMMENDATIONS FOR AMENDMENTS
Proposal for a Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Directives (EU) 2018/2001, (EU) 2019/944, (EU) 2024/1788 as regards acceleration of permit-granting procedures
Amendments to Directive (EU) 2018/2001 (Renewable Energy Directive)
Amendment 1
Recital 4 Point a (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
Amendment
Accelerated permitting procedures shall ensure early and effective public participation, including access to relevant information and meaningful consultation, in accordance with Union law;
Amendment 2
Recital 11 Point a (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
Amendment
The simplification of permitting procedures must not lead to any lowering of environmental protection standards or to a weakening of public participation requirements established under Union environmental law;
Amendment 3
Recital 16 Point a (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
Amendment
In order to accelerate permit-granting procedures while ensuring public acceptance and territorial coherence, Member States should support local and regional authorities through a local energy action and delivery (LEAD) approach. Proximity-based administrative support and coordination, with an emphasis on value-added local participation, can significantly reduce delays and improve the quality of permit decisions. The LEAD framework should furthermore promote the incorporation of landscape and cultural impact assessments at the earliest stages of project planning, ensuring that local level energy solutions remain compatible with the preservation of artistic and natural heritage. This will require specific financial support to build capacity for such local participation at the relevant level.
Reason
The LEAD framework will enhance regional capacity in permitting, ensuring LRAs can effectively implement and manage permit workflows.
Amendment 4
Recital 16 Point b (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
Amendment
(16b)
Accelerated permitting for grid infrastructure should be based on integrated energy system planning that ensures coherence between electricity networks, heating and cooling systems, energy-efficiency measures and demand-side flexibility. Involving regional and local planning authorities early in the process can improve project design, local participation, public acceptance and cost-effectiveness as well as ensure that planning takes into account the specific characteristics and protection requirements of landscapes and sites of artistic or historical interest.

Member States shall set up a local energy action and delivery (LEAD) framework to support the implementation of local production, flexibility measures and permit-granting procedures at local and regional levels. Such a framework shall include mandatory consultation mechanisms for authorities responsible for safeguarding artistic and landscape heritage at the initial stages of all grid and renewable energy projects that may exert a significant visual or territorial impact. The LEAD framework shall provide technical, administrative, financial and coordination support to local and regional authorities involved in local production and flexibility measures, as well as permitting procedures under this Directive, standardised tools and capacity-building measures. The Commission shall publish implementing guidance within 12 months of entry into force of this Directive to support Member States in implementing local, proximity-based solutions, including in the areas of energy production and flexibility, and in streamlining permitting procedures.
Reason
The amendment strengthens the role of local and regional authorities in education, facilitation and public dialogue, in line with subsidiarity and ensuring effective coordination with existing local procedures and proportionate implementation without undue administrative or financial burdens

Article 1 – Paragraph 3 – Article 15d – Paragraph 6 (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
CoR amendment
Member States shall ensure that the competent authorities designated under this Article coordinate permit-granting procedures with national, regional and local energy and land use planning processes, including those reflected in national energy and climate plans and relevant regional energy strategies.
This coordination shall ensure that grid infrastructure permitting considers integrated energy system planning, including electricity, heating and cooling, energy efficiency, demand-side flexibility and specific local solutions relating to production and flexibility, as well as land use planning.
Amendment 10
Article 1 – Paragraph 3 – Article 15d – Paragraph 7 (new)
Text proposed by the European Commission
Amendment
Member States shall ensure that the costs of network development are fairly shared among all users, while fully protecting low-income households. In addition, Member States shall ensure that regions with above-average shares of renewable energy production are not disproportionately burdened by network development costs, in particular where such investment serves cross-regional or cross-border interests. In such cases, cost-sharing mechanisms shall reflect the distribution of the benefits across regions and Member States, taking account of: (a) the extent to which the grid infrastructure serves multiple regions or enables cross-border energy flows; (b) how much the host region contributes to the EU’s climate objectives through the production of renewable energy; (c) the need to avoid competitive disadvantages for energy-intensive industries in regions with high levels of renewable energy production; (d) the principle of solidarity and fair cost sharing as set out in the TEN-E Regulation.
Reason
Integrating large amounts of renewable energy requires significant investment in grid infrastructure. This infrastructure is not used purely for regional supply, but the costs are mainly borne by regional consumers.

II.     POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS
THE EUROPEAN COMMITTEE OF THE REGIONS (COR)
1.
welcomes the presentation of the European Grids Package and the Energy Highways initiative as an important step towards modernising the EU energy framework; underlines that achieving the clean energy transition requires urgent action, substantial public and private investment and enhanced coordination to speed up the implementation of energy infrastructure projects, while preventing lengthy permitting procedures and cost overruns; emphasises the need to ensure the resilience, safety and reliability of the power system against natural disasters such as floods, wildfires, droughts and storms, but also from external attacks or hybrid threats; calls on the Commission, Member States and national authorities to support grid operators in increasing the resilience of the grid system; underlines the need to support the work on climate risks assessments, protection of critical infrastructure, cybersecurity tools and the necessary investments to guarantee grids preparedness and recovery;
2.
regrets that the proposed centralised scheme, relying largely on a top-down approach, does not sufficiently consider the contribution of local and regional authorities to the identification and planning of local needs for grid infrastructure and to the development of local production and flexibility solutions which help mitigate against excessive infrastructure requirements, thereby limiting the democratisation of the energy system through active local participation, shared ownership and place-based decision-making;
3.
stresses the urgent need to strengthen the resilience of the Union’s electricity grids, in light of recent largescale disruptions, including the blackout affecting the Iberian Peninsula as well as incidents in Berlin and parts of the Czech Republic, which illustrate the exposure of Europe’s interconnected power system to environmental stress, capacity constraints, technical failures and deliberate human interference;
4.
calls for the acceleration of permitting procedures for renewable energy projects, recalling that the 2025 Committee of the Regions Annual Report on the State of Regions and Cities identifies administrative delays as a persistent barrier to timely deployment; urges the establishment of an EU-wide digital permitting system to reduce administrative burdens and enable faster and more efficient local approvals; calls for the swift implementation of Renewables Acceleration Areas;
5.
recommends that the European Commission and Member States formally integrate local and regional authorities (LRAs) into the governance, planning, and implementation of the European Energy Highways Initiative. The Commission shall ensure that the governance of the Energy Highways Initiative upholds environmental safeguards, public consultation and social acceptance, and that simplification and acceleration do not undermine environmental protection, biodiversity, landscape considerations or citizen engagement;
6.
welcomes the guidance on efficient grid connections and calls on the European Commission to adopt binding recommendations or regulatory principles that remove administrative barriers, accelerate project implementation, and ensure that grid development supports local energy production and regional decarbonisation objectives;
7.
underlines the need to foster cooperation on energy technology and policies for the clean transition, especially in securing stable and secure European supply chains for critical power grids components; recalls the need to respect the principle of technological neutrality and to be applied by TSOs/DSOs in their approach to electricity generation, including RES, nuclear, gas, and also to take into account various impacts on both onshore and offshore infrastructure;
8.
underlines that efforts to simplify the TEN-E Regulation and accelerate permitting procedures must not undermine environmental standards, public consultations or the protection of local communities and biodiversity; calls for further fragmentation of EU procedural law to be prevented and for permit-granting procedures in the various areas of EU law to be made as uniform as possible;
Local energy action and delivery
9.
calls for a local energy action and delivery (LEAD) framework to support the implementation of permit-granting procedures and complementary solutions at local and regional levels; emphasises that the framework should be part of an Action Plan to empower local and regional authorities to design, adapt and manage permitting solutions in line with local needs and territorial specificities; stresses the need for targeted technical assistance and capacity-building that is locally driven, including one-stop-shops support, standardised yet flexible guidance, and interoperable digital tools under local control; encourages the creation of One Stop Shops to facilitate peer-to-peer exchange and the sharing of best practices; calls for adequate, flexible funding aligned with existing EU energy and cohesion instruments, ensuring that EU support strengthens local decision-making;
10.
calls for tailored support for territories with specific constraints. The LEAD framework shall provide targeted measures for small municipalities, islands and outermost regions including advisory services and priority access to funding for local infrastructure and staff costs in line with CoR evidence on funding access barriers;
11.
calls for local and regional authorities to be formally recognised as key partners in planning, advocacy, permitting and monitoring, which is indispensable for aligning grid expansion with local development priorities and climate adaptation needs;
12.
regrets that, despite the presentation of the grids package, its territorial impacts have not been adequately assessed; calls on the European Commission to ensure that the implementation of the package systematically integrates local and regional decarbonisation plans and is supported by robust territorial impact assessments, in order to align grid development with regional needs, spatial planning and local implementation capacities;
13.
calls for local and regional authorities to be mandatory and systematically involved in regional energy-grid planning bodies and in all consultation phases of the Ten-Year Network Development Plans (TYNDPs), ensuring close coordination with transmission and distribution system operators, other regions, and Member States; stresses that reinforcing the regional dimension in energy infrastructure planning is crucial to ensure coherence between local energy policies, grid investments, and electrification objectives;;
14.
believes that local and regional authorities must have a formal and permanent role in energy planning at both EU and national levels, including a complementary role in local production and flexibility solutions; urges the Commission to invite the Committee of the Regions to participate in the Energy Union Task Force  ( 1 ) , ensuring that the local dimension is part of the EU energy decision-making process;
15.
underlines that the effective and smooth implementation of the European Green Deal and current energy policies depends on well-equipped local and regional energy agencies, appropriately funded local solutions and advocacy and one-stop shops  ( 2 ) ;
Energy affordability – the cost of electricity
16.
reiterates that energy affordability is at the heart of the energy transition. Given the crucial role that grids play in integrating renewable energy and supporting electrification, grid development must provide real added value while demonstrably helping to bring down energy bills and tackling energy poverty and affordability; underlines that the costs of grid expansion must be shared fairly among all users, with households on low incomes fully protected; stresses the importance of ensuring that no territory is placed at a disproportionate financial disadvantage when grid investments primarily serve wider regional, cross-border or system-level benefits.; emphasises that all major energy consumers should contribute in a manner that reflects the impact of their demand on the electricity system, in line with principles of fairness and cost-reflectiveness; stresses that addressing grid congestion and accelerating flexibility solutions is essential to avoid the curtailment and waste of renewable electricity and reiterates that the infrastructure planning should align generation and storage capacity with areas of highest energy demand;
17.
points out that an estimated EUR 1,2 trillion will be needed for the EU’s electricity grids between now and 2040, and that such an investment must be subject to rigorous cost benefit analyses, demonstrably contribute to the phase-out of fossil fuels, and must prove a benefit to consumers in terms of affordable and lower electricity costs and enhanced economic benefits at local level; calls for the territorial distribution of benefits to be reflected in cost–benefit analyses and for solidarity-based cost-sharing mechanisms to apply to infrastructure investments serving supra-regional or cross-border purposes;
18.
acknowledges the European Commission’s proposal to triple the budget of the Connecting Europe Facility, which represents a significant step forward in financing the energy transition; stresses, however, that the energy transition is not merely a technical or financial challenge, but a transformative process that requires deep engagement and ownership at the regional and local levels;
19.
calls on the Commission, when revising the TEN-E Regulation, to lay down specific solidarity-based funding mechanisms for cross-border and cross-regional grid infrastructure, ensuring that the costs are shared fairly in line with the geographical distribution of the benefits; suggests that the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF-E) should prioritise projects that help regions where renewable energy production is high to integrate it into the network and to expand transmission capacity; stresses that these regions play a key role in decarbonising the European energy system and that their infrastructure investment benefits Europe as a whole;
20.
points out that low energy costs are a major locational and competitive advantage. Given the ambitious digital policy objectives and the need to scale up data centres – which are seen as critical infrastructure for the European resilience and competitiveness of digital technologies and at the same time offer significant potential for increased sustainability – remedial actions such as electricity price compensation should be explored. In this context, the CEEAG list also needs to be modernised and adapted to the requirements of the digital age;
21.
calls on the European Commission to prioritise support for small- and medium-scale distribution grid projects and local energy production close to end users, following the ‘local-to-local’ approach, in order to reinforce local energy sovereignty, reduce grid congestion, and maximise the territorial benefits of energy deployment;
22.
stresses that promoting energy communities requires dedicated measures, under transparent and non-discriminatory conditions, to facilitate their access to the grid, incentives for local production and flexibility solutions which minimise the requirement for new grids, and support for the optimal use of available capacity; underlines the importance of strengthening regional and local acceptance by clearly demonstrating the socio-economic, environmental and territorial benefits of energy communities, including local value creation and citizen participation; emphasises that such measures should support and accelerate the development of a decentralised, resilient and consumer-oriented electricity system;
Addressing grid congestion
23.
supports the Commission’s proposal to replace the ‘first come, first served’ model with a ‘first ready, first-served’ principle for grid connections, prioritising mature projects, projects generating qualified jobs and preventing speculation and grid connection hoarding by disincentivising applications for connection where these are not substantiated by a solid project or where the developer cannot show sufficient commitment to the realisation of a project as possible criteria for connection rights; and underlines that energy communities and local energy sharing projects should, where appropriate, be given priority access to grid capacity, unless a clear system efficiency justification requires otherwise; stresses that prioritisation should reflect local and regional needs and therefore welcomes the Dutch framework, which allocates grid access based on security and societal value criteria;
24.
states that contracts for difference (CfD) must be adapted to the specific needs and capacities of municipalities, allowing local authorities to directly invest in co-owned renewable energy projects, reinvesting revenues into local energy efficiency projects and grid upgrades;
25.
states that incentives and market mechanisms for flexibility through digitalisation and smart technologies at the local level (distribution system) are critical for maximising the efficiency of the existing distribution grid and for avoiding excessive build costs for inefficient new infrastructure;
26.
points out that islands, mountainous areas and outermost regions face specific challenges in grid capacity and congestion that hinder their energy transition and increase costs for consumers; calls on the Commission and Member States to adopt tailored regulatory and investment frameworks that address these specificities;
27.
points out that electricity systems in the outermost regions are isolated and cannot be connected to the continental European grid, which limits their flexibility and makes it difficult for them to integrate clean energy from the outside. In this regard, points out that investment in renewable energy infrastructure and in energy storage is essential for ensuring security of supply and optimising renewable energy in these regions, and stresses that the costs involved exceed the amount that these regions can invest on their own;
28.
stresses that the outermost regions cannot be excluded from EU policies and funds for the energy transition as this would jeopardise their social and territorial cohesion and their transition to a carbon-neutral economy;
29.
recognises the strategic role of large urban and metropolitan areas as key flexibility nodes in the electricity system, where active demand management, the digitalisation of distribution grids, storage and efficient electrification can reduce the need for new infrastructure, improve system stability and strengthen Europe’s energy autonomy;;
Fostering public acceptance in the energy transition
30.
highlights the fact that the meaningful participation of local and regional authorities is not optional, but a precondition for social acceptance; stresses that local and regional authorities must be involved at the earliest stages of raising awareness, advocacy and planning, with structured and binding consultation mechanisms to reduce opposition to accelerating project delivery;
31.
underlines the strategic importance of prioritising ‘made in Europe’ technologies and equipment in grid deployment to reduce dependency and to reinforce EU industry, stimulating local economic development; calls on EU and national authorities to align public procurement standards and certification frameworks to scale up European technologies. However, legal demands must be proportionate, with a limited administrative burden and not infringe on the basic function of procurement to achieve contracts and supplies according to the needs and means of the procuring authority;
32.
calls for a stronger role for local and regional authorities in education, facilitation, and public dialogue on energy and grid projects, in full respect of the principle of subsidiarity and emphasises that this must be coordinated with existing local procedures and implemented in a proportionate way, avoiding unnecessary administrative or financial burdens on local authorities;
33.
stresses that social acceptance depends on communities delivering and benefiting from local energy infrastructure; calls for enforceable benefit-sharing and proposes a mandatory scheme for all projects above 5 MW; energy projects respecting benefit-sharing principles should be prioritised in permitting and grid connection.
Brussels, 5 March 2026.
